tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: Begin with Nook’s project overview and product context. They describe a community app for profiles, friendships, feeds, conversations, and games, with Code Arena as its current playable game and first-game baseline. Keep this map in view as you trace the client, platform services, match runtime, judge, and deployment layers.

tour.title: Game Service Entry
tour.description: Following the Code Arena path introduced above, the highest-ranked code entry candidate boots the NestJS game service and starts listening on its configured port. The application module composes the game feature with health checks, while the game module registers its controllers, gateways, and providers. This boundary leads into the match flow and live-play components explored later.

tour.title: Browser and Identity
tour.description: The client root layout wraps routes in shared providers, and its authentication provider maintains the signed-in session and authenticated-request helpers. Typed client requests reach the User service authentication endpoints, whose service owns credentials, OAuth, JWT sessions, refresh-token rotation, and password resets. This identity path enables the protected Chat and Play experiences that follow.

tour.title: Conversations and Profiles
tour.description: With account identity established, the client chat workspace brings together conversations, groups, presence, history, and attachments. The Chat controller and service implement those authenticated routes and their persistence rules, while a RabbitMQ consumer synchronizes User account events into Chat records and feed membership. The integration guide explains the ordering, replay behavior, and limits of that service boundary.

tour.title: Shared Arena Rules
tour.description: The Arena packages define the vocabulary used by the runtime: match records, lifecycle phases, player readiness, and results. Scoring validates weighted hidden-test groups and tie-breaks, while transition helpers decide when running, submitting, editing, and revealing are allowed. The problem-bank schema sets the record shape for statements, examples, tests, starter code, and provenance.

tour.title: Match State and Rooms
tour.description: Building on those shared rules, the lobby manages queues and private rooms, while the engine owns authoritative match state across rounds, submissions, evaluations, collaboration, presence, and forfeits. Match authority serializes mutations and checks participant membership; round lifecycle applies transitions, publishes reveals, and computes results. The file bank loads the versioned problems that players receive.

tour.title: Realtime Team Play
tour.description: The Game service adapts the match core to HTTP and live connections. Its match gateway sends snapshots and player actions, while separate collaboration and team-chat gateways enforce the 2v2 editor and chat boundaries. In the browser, ArenaWorkspace coordinates editor state, collaboration, runs, submissions, readiness, and round transitions.

tour.title: Sandboxed Judging
tour.description: When a player runs or submits code, the Game service’s judge factory selects the configured backend. The Arena package provides isolated one-shot container execution and a worker adapter, while the worker entry point wires Docker readiness, a bounded queue, and its HTTP server. The queue caps concurrent jobs and applies separate wait and execution timeouts.

tour.title: Game Event Delivery
tour.description: Match lifecycle updates also cross service boundaries: the Game publisher emits sanitized public events, and the shared event contract gives them stable payload shapes. Chat validates those events before applying conversation notifications, then the client parser recognizes and titles the resulting messages. This connects match starts, results, and cancelled challenges to Nook’s chat experience.

tour.title: Persistence Contracts
tour.description: The services keep separate relational ownership: the User schema holds account and authentication records, while the Chat schema owns conversations and messages. Chat’s GameChallenge record links a private Arena room code to its conversation and optional match ID; the Arena PostgreSQL store persists match, submission, reveal, collaboration, and lobby state. These boundaries distinguish game state from cross-service conversation links.

tour.title: Deployment and Monitoring
tour.description: The Compose stack assembles the application services, databases, broker, storage, gateway, backups, and monitoring. Nginx terminates local TLS and routes frontend, API, realtime, and MinIO traffic; the infrastructure guide covers environment ownership and operations. The monitoring Compose layer and Prometheus configuration provide the observability services and alert evaluation.

tour.title: Verification Evidence
tour.description: Finish with the repeatable verification guide and the recorded two-client demonstration. The evidence describes challenge and match notifications, reload persistence, and the limits of what that run proves. Game, Chat, and client tests cover payload privacy, notification persistence, and message parsing, showing which integration behaviors also have automated checks.
